title: Behavior Change Hidden Inside a Structural Refactoring (Two Hats)
pattern: A single diff or commit that performs a behavior-preserving structural change (rename, extract variable/constant/function/trait/parameter object, inline, move a function or file, flatten into guard clauses, delete dead code or comments, reformat, deduplicate into a shared helper, chain constructors, normalize symmetry, replace a type code with an enum, wrap in an adapter, split query from modifier) also changes observable behavior: altered constants, defaults or fallback literals, changed predicates or operators, new or removed validation, different return/error semantics (`Option` to `Result`, new `unwrap`/panic paths, new default on missing key), added enum variants or trait methods, extra parameters, or new transformations of inputs.
why_bad: Refactoring and changing behavior are different activities with different verification: a refactoring is checked by existing tests continuing to pass unchanged, a behavior change needs new or updated tests and a reviewer's judgment. Mixing them ("wearing both hats") hides the behavior change in a diff that reads as mechanical cleanup, so reviewers skim past a flipped `<`/`<=` or a changed constant. When something breaks, the failure cannot be attributed to either the restructuring or the new logic, and neither half can be reverted independently. For file moves, content edits also defeat version-control rename detection, so history and blame are lost.
detection: Read the removed and added lines together. Identify hunks whose shape is a structural refactoring (same logic reappearing under a new name or location, an expression replaced by a named variable or constant, nested conditionals replaced by guard clauses, duplicated blocks replaced by calls to a new helper, whitespace-only or layout-only changes, a moved file or function, a new trait/enum/parameter struct/adapter/getter wrapping existing code), then check whether the refactored form is semantically equivalent to the original for all inputs. Flag when it is not: a literal or default value differs, a relational or boolean operator or predicate set differs, a call site's arguments differ after consolidation, the signature or error type changes during a move or rename, new variants/methods/parameters appear, a panic path or I/O side effect is introduced, or input is transformed differently. Flag renamed or moved files whose content changes beyond import and path updates. Do not flag a diff that makes only a behavior change, or only a refactoring.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Refactorings that preserve behavior exactly (a constant extracted with its original value, guard clauses with a logically equivalent predicate, a moved function with an identical signature), and behavior changes submitted alone. Also acceptable: a change where the refactoring and the behavior change are separate commits in the same pull request, trivially small fixes in projects that explicitly accept combined changes, and mechanical follow-through a behavior change requires (updating call sites for a new parameter is part of that change, not a hidden one).
source: Martin Fowler, *Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code* (1999), Ch. 2 "The Two Hats", Ch. 6–11; Kent Beck, *Tidy First?* (2023), Ch. 1–3, 13, 15–17 ("Separate Tidying"); Titus Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* (2020), Ch. 16, 18, 22; Heather Adkins et al., *Building Secure and Reliable Systems* (2020), Ch. 7; Joshua Kerievsky, *Refactoring to Patterns* (2004), Ch. 6, 7, 11; Michael Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004), Ch. 25; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Ch. 24.
